evidence.summary: Learning objective and scope: For 'Software Engineering', the learner can roadmap table of Professional Python Core topics (comprehensions/unpacking/slicing, iterable/iterator/generator, closures/decorators, exceptions/context managers, dataclasses/enums, typing/generics/Protocol, packaging, concurrency) and a Software Engineering roadmap (Git/review depth, pytest strategy, Ruff/mypy, packaging, system-layer knowledge: HTTP, SQL, Linux, security, CI/CD, containers).

Iterable/iterator/generator, closures/decorators, and context managers are framed as NOT yet mastered — future Professional Core material -- confirmed accurate and non-contradictory: grepped scripts/build_chapter_01.py..build_chapter_23.py for 'yield' (only 1 incidental occurrence, in build_chapter_22.py, not a taught generator lesson) and 'context manager'/'контекстный менеджер' (zero occurrences outside Chapter 24 itself) — the book genuinely never teaches writing generators or custom context managers before Chapter 24, so presenting them as forward material is accurate, not an overclaim

Decorators are framed as Professional-Core future material even though '@property setter', '@dataclass', and '@app.route' decorators are used/shown earlier (ch13, ch14, ch22) -- confirmed non-contradictory: all three earlier occurrences are passing uses of existing decorators (framework/stdlib-provided), never a lesson on writing a custom decorator with closures — which is exactly the skill Chapter 24 frames as still-to-learn ('Вы сохраняете сигнатуру и понимаете порядок вызовов')

dataclasses/enums framed as Professional-Core material despite @dataclass being explained in Chapter 14 and Enum used in chapters 17-21 -- not a contradiction: Chapter 24's framing is 'inварианты не растворены в наборе строковых литералов', i.e. deeper/more disciplined use, consistent with dataclasses/enums having only been introduced at an OOP-basics level earlier — soft continuity, not a factual conflict

'Typing, aliases, generics, Protocol' framed as forward Core material despite basic function-annotation type hints being taught in Chapter 13 -- confirmed non-contradictory: Chapter 13 teaches only basic parameter/return annotations and explicitly notes 'аннотация ничего не отменяет' (runtime is unaffected) — generics, type aliases and Protocol are a distinct, deeper topic never taught earlier, and Chapter 24's own text ('Вы помните, что аннотации сами по себе не проверяются') presupposes exactly the Chapter 13 knowledge, correctly building on it rather than contradicting it

Software Engineering system-layer capability_map (HTTP, SQL, Linux/shell, security, CI/CD, containers) framed as knowledge 'around' Python code, not claimed as already taught -- confirmed: framing is explicitly forward-looking ('Знания вокруг Python-кода' / 'В реальном проекте... взаимодействует с'), consistent with the book's actual scope
Ruff and mypy recommended as the lint/type-check tools to standardize on -- confirmed both are real, actively maintained, currently-standard Python tooling choices as of the audit date; not stale
